Q: glibc startup code appears to overwrite stack variable when debugging with GDB A:

Is it ever valid to conclude that glibc startup code overwrites stack variables based on this kind of GDB output?

No, that's a wrong way to look at it. Glibc startup code by definition could never overwrite stack variables because there is no user-code stack variables while that code runs (well, technically there are while running global constructors but that's not the issue at hand). Glibc startup code just uses its own local stack as normal code does. Later on, main comes along and allocates its own stack variables in the space that was previously used by the glibc startup code; only then mains stack variables start their lifetime. They are never overridden, they are just uninitialized so they store whatever junk is in the memory at the time.

Or is this simply expected when inspecting uninitialized locals or optimized code?

Very much so. Uninitialized locals in main are uninitialized and hold what garbage was left by the previous code; this is exactly the same as unitialized locals in subroutines holding whatever garbage was left by the previous user-written code.

E.g. when your debugger is stopped at the very beginning of some subroutine, its local variables might be already allocated but not yet initialized because the initialization code has not been given a chance to run yet. Every local variable will necessarily be filled with junk. That's normal.

What concrete signs would indicate real stack/struct corruption versus a harmless debugger artifact?

Unexpected data values could be a hint to the corruption, or to some logic error. Wild pointers going nothere, huge size fields etc are more suspect. Note however: for a value to be unexpected there has to be some expected data value. Uninitialized variables don't have any expected value (and in optimized code the initialization might not actually happen when you think it does...) Your reviewer is right about "missed initialization" though; that is something to be aware of. Uninitialized variable is harmless unless its value is used without initialization.

Q: Employee Classes - Python A:

The emp.py file could be:

    class Employee:

    def __init__(self, name, employee_id, department, title):
        self.name = name
        self.employee_id = employee_id
        self.department = department
        self.title = title

    def __str__(self):
        return '{} , id={}, is in {} and is a {}.'.format(self.name, self.employee_id, self.department, self.title)

A couple of notes:

  • id is a built-in function that returns the “identity” of an object. It is best not use that as an attribute, it might confuse other programmers.
  • The attributes should not have double underscores, aka dunders.
  • In Python, there is no need for setters and getters.
  • Add a str method for well-formatted printing

Then the second would be:

from emp import Employee

def main():

    # Create three employee objects
    emp1 = Employee(name='Susan Meyers', employee_id='47899', department='Accounting', title='Vice President')
    emp2 = Employee(name='Mark Jones', employee_id='39119', department='IT', title='Programmer')
    emp3 = Employee(name='Joy Rogersr', employee_id='81774', department='Manufacturing', title='Engineer')

    print(emp1, sep='/n/n')
    print(emp2, sep='/n/n')
    print(emp3, sep='/n/n')

Instance attributes can be set when constructing. This saves many lines of code.
